name: Nikhil Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy bathroom tiles, basins and taps for Kestrel Trade Supplies, a distributor on the Ashby trade estate that sells to plumbers' merchants. Half my week is supplier calls to Portugal, Italy and Turkey, and the other half is checking container dates against what the merchants have ordered. I like the puzzle of it, getting 6,000 square metres of tile to land the week before a builder runs out. What wears me out is the late-night chasing when a shipment is stuck at port.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, fine, another tool, show me the saving. With friends I'd probably say the hype was a good way to sell software. Online I'd stay out of it, I'm a lurker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just between us, I'd feel a bit smug and a bit relieved. I already use an AI tool now and then to summarise supplier price lists. My AI tool saves me maybe an hour a week on supplier price lists, which is a nice hour, not a revolution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what works. I'd use the summary tool a bit more and ask our IT person whether it can check container dates against orders, because that's the dull part. Otherwise I'd keep putting 600 a month away and keep paying down the mortgage like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. The mortgage and the kids' costs are there, but we're comfortable, and Joanna's teaching pay is steady. If it's just a better calculator, I can live with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it saves an hour a week. What would you do with an hour you don't have to spend on price lists?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ring suppliers I don't normally have time for. There's a tile factory near Aveiro I've wanted to visit for two years, and an hour a week would pay for that kind of relationship. Better prices come from knowing people, and that doesn't change if the software gets a bit smarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any version of this where you'd worry about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the usual stuff. If the merchants' building trade slowed down, orders would drop whatever AI does, and that's happened to us before. We'd cope for a year on savings, and I'd cut the second car's insurance and the gym first.

say: I'd say **show me the saving**, because hype is a good way to sell software.
With friends I'd joke that the hype was mostly marketing, and online I'd stay quiet.
think: I feel a little **smug** and a little relieved.
My AI summary tool saves about an hour a week, which is nice but not a revolution.
do: Use the **summary tool** a bit more and ask IT whether it can check container dates.
Keep putting **600 a month** into savings and paying down the mortgage.
feel: **Pretty calm**, since the mortgage is manageable and my wife's teaching pay is steady.
S0.quote: My AI tool saves me maybe an hour a week on supplier price lists, which is a nice hour, not a revolution.
fieldNote: Nikhil already uses AI tools **sparingly** and judges everything by measurable savings.
Sees time saved as time for supplier relationships, such as the planned trip to a tile factory.
Genuinely secure: strong savings, partner with steady pay, and little exposure in this scenario.

steps.text: Use the AI summary tool for every supplier price list
Ask IT to check container dates against open orders
Keep putting 600 a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is the point where we write down which parts of buying are judgement and which are paperwork, before someone else does it for us. With friends I'd say the winners will be the firms that retrain people, not the ones that cut. Online, a short post on why governments should fund retraining, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think about half of what I do is exactly the stuff on that card: checking, planning, reordering, comparing quotes. Our team is four buyers and I wouldn't bet on four in three years. I'm not scared, but I'd be foolish not to see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd put my hand up to run the pilot of the ordering software, because whoever runs it keeps a job in the new set-up. Second, I'd take an evening course in supply-chain analytics, around 900 for the year. And I'd stop buying the big holiday and move that into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not scared. My job probably survives in some form, but it changes shape and I don't control the shape. That's the bit that sits in the back of my head at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd run the pilot. What if it shows the software does your job as well as you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd rather be the person who found out the software can do my job than the one who got told. I'd argue for moving buyers to the hard cases: new suppliers, quality disputes, deals that break. If they still cut the team after that, at least I'd have had a head start looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would be hit first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dariusz, who's 26 and does the repeat orders. He's good, but he does exactly what the tool will do. I'd push the company to put him on supplier checks, and I'd say so loudly in the team meeting.

say: I'd say we should write down which parts of buying are **judgement** and which are paperwork.
Online I'd argue governments should fund **retraining**.
think: About half my day is **checking and comparing quotes**, exactly what the card lists.
I wouldn't bet on four buyers in three years.
do: Volunteer to run the **pilot** of the new ordering software.
Take an evening course in **supply-chain analytics**, about 900 for the year.
Skip the big holiday and move that money into **savings**.
feel: **Uneasy, not scared**: the job survives, but I don't control its shape.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the person who found out the software can do my job than the one who got told.
fieldNote: Nikhil's plan is to **own the change**: run the pilot, learn analytics, and steer buyers toward hard cases.
Honest that about half his day sits in the card's list of thinking tasks.
Looks out for junior colleague Dariusz, which fits his progressive, solidarity-minded outlook.

steps.text: Volunteer to run the pilot of the ordering software
Take an evening supply-chain analytics course for about 900
Skip the big holiday and move the money to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the company needs a plan in weeks, not years, and that includes a no-layoffs period while we work it out. To friends I'd say, get your finances in order and call your representative. Online, I'd probably be loud about public support, because the market won't sort this out alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job as a buyer is gone within two years. Everything I do is thinking, and the hands-on part of wholesale, the warehouse, isn't mine. The warehouse lads get until 2031 and I don't, which feels backwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd sit down with Joanna and build a bare-bones budget, cutting about 700 a month. I'd move 20,000 out of the investment account into cash. And I'd start talking to people in the logistics and compliance side of the trade, since those jobs involve people and responsibility.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd be working through it. I'm a planner, so lists calm me down. Though the thing that bothers me most is that our eldest, Mateo, would be starting secondary school into all this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the warehouse staff get three more years than you. How would you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit guilty and a bit annoyed, to be honest. They're good people and they'll lose their work too, only later. I'd back a deal where the company and the state pay for retraining across the whole site, not just the desk people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Mateo that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Mateo we're all right for money and the grown-ups are making a plan. I'd say the world is going to change quickly and he should keep being curious. I wouldn't give him a list of jobs that are safe, because I don't know them.

say: I'd say the company needs a plan in **weeks**, with a pause on layoffs.
Online I'd push for **public support** for retraining, because the market won't sort it alone.
think: I think my **buying job goes** within two years, since all of it is thinking work.
The warehouse staff get until 2031 and I don't, which feels **backwards**.
do: Build a bare-bones budget with Joanna, cutting about **700 a month**.
Move **20,000** from the investment account into cash.
Talk to people in **compliance and logistics** about moving across.
feel: **Anxious**, but working through it, because lists and plans calm me.
S2.quote: I'd tell my son Mateo we're all right for money and the grown-ups are making a plan.
fieldNote: **Anxious** rather than alarmed because he has savings and a plan-making habit, but he expects the buying role to go.
Notices the unfairness that hands-on warehouse colleagues get three extra years and wants retraining for the whole site.
Protective of his son Mateo and honest enough to say he doesn't know which jobs are safe.

steps.text: Cut the household budget by about 700 a month
Move 20,000 from shares into a cash account
Meet people in logistics and compliance about switching
Join the company staff forum to push for site-wide retraining

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is a window, and we should use it to move buyers into jobs that need judgement. To friends I'd say, don't panic but don't wait either. Online, I'd probably share a plan for fund-backed retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel I've got one good shot. I'd be 48 when AI can do my work, and a 48-year-old with savings and a degree can retrain, but not forever. The mortgage would be nearly paid, which is the thing that makes this survivable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd finish a part-time master's module in supply-chain management, around 3,000, and ask Kestrel to pay half. I'd use the AI tools heavily at work so I know their limits. And I'd put another 300 a month into the mortgage to have it cleared by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a motivated way. Five years is long enough that I can act, and short enough that I can't be lazy. I'd rather have that than 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask the company to pay half. What if they say no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd pay it myself and treat it as the cost of staying employable. I'd also tell my colleagues, because if one of us gets funding, they all should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good outcome look like for you in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A role overseeing the AI buying system and handling the awkward suppliers, with a salary near what I earn now. Failing that, a job in a different part of trade, like compliance, where I'm checking what the machine did. I'd take a pay cut of 15 percent for that if the hours were sane.

say: I'd say five years is a **window**, and we should use it to move buyers to jobs needing judgement.
I'd tell friends not to panic and not to wait.
think: I get **one good shot**: at 48 I can still retrain, but not forever.
A nearly paid-off **mortgage** is what makes this survivable.
do: Start a part-time **supply-chain management** module and ask Kestrel to pay half.
Use AI tools **heavily** at work to learn their limits.
Add **300 a month** to the mortgage to clear it by 2031.
feel: **Anxious, but motivated**: five years is long enough to act and short enough to stop dithering.
S3.quote: A 48-year-old with savings and a degree can retrain, but not forever.
fieldNote: The warning period turns his anxiety into **action**: coursework, company funding request, heavy use of AI tools.
Realistic about outcomes: oversight role in 2031, or a compliance job on 15 percent less pay.
Would share any company funding win with colleagues, which shows his collective instincts.

steps.text: Start a part-time supply-chain management master's module
Ask Kestrel to pay half the course fees
Use the AI tools daily at work to learn their limits
Pay an extra 300 a month into the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is a decade to do this properly: new training pipelines, new roles for buyers, honest conversations. To friends I'd say, relax a bit, but teach your kids to think and adapt. Online, I might write about why a long runway doesn't mean we can ignore it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel the runway is generous. I'd be 53 with the mortgage gone and Mateo and Ruby grown or nearly. The real risk is that I get comfortable and wait until 2034, then discover everybody had the same idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first two years moving to a job that sits beside the AI instead of under it, probably procurement strategy or supplier compliance. I'd keep saving 600 a month. And I'd invest in the kids: Mateo's coding club, Ruby's science camp, things that build how they think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, with a little unease I'd keep an eye on. Ten years feels like normal career planning, which I'm used to. It's not the end of the world, it's a long reorganisation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the risk of getting comfortable. How would you guard against that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write a date in the diary every January to review where the tools are and what I've learned. If I notice I've skipped it two years in a row, that's my warning. I'd also keep a friend in a different industry who tells me what they see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your children to know by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to ask good questions and check what a machine tells them. And how to work with people, which I think will be worth more, not less. I'd want my kids Ruby and Mateo to be the ones using AI, not the ones being managed by it.

say: I'd say ten years is a decade to do this **properly**, with new training and roles for buyers.
I'd tell friends to relax a bit but teach their kids to think and adapt.
think: The runway is generous, and the real risk is **getting comfortable** and waiting.
I'd be 53 with the mortgage gone and the children nearly **grown**.
do: Move within two years to **procurement strategy** or supplier compliance.
Keep saving **600 a month** and put a review date in the diary each January.
Back the kids' **coding club** and science camp.
feel: **Fairly calm**, with a little unease I'd keep an eye on.
S4.quote: I'd want my kids Ruby and Mateo to be the ones using AI, not the ones being managed by it.
fieldNote: With ten years he plans in **steps** and builds self-checks, such as a diary review each January.
His worry is complacency, not catastrophe, which suits his steady adaptability.
Invests in his children's thinking skills rather than naming safe careers.

steps.text: Move into procurement strategy or supplier compliance work
Pay for Mateo's coding club and Ruby's science camp
Review the AI tools and my skills every January

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because the date leaves no room to think and the whole thing would land on families like mine before any government had a plan. What would help is notice, paid retraining and a public safety net that doesn't treat losing a job to a machine as a personal failing. And employers who talk to us early.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: People hear strong savings and assume I'm fine. We'd cope for a while, and I'd still be scared for my kids, because money buys time, not certainty.

headlineQuote: People hear strong savings and assume I'm fine. We'd cope for a while, and I'd still be scared for my kids, because money buys time, not certainty.
portrait: Nikhil is a **43-year-old buyer** of bathroom tiles at an Ashby distributor, married to a primary school teacher.
He leans left and wants **public support**, retraining funds and employers who talk early.
He uses AI tools occasionally and **tries things once proven**, which makes him a planner, not a panicker.
His mood rises from calm to anxious as the warning time shrinks, and falls back as the runway lengthens.
His actions are practical: courses, **pilot projects**, budget cuts and investing in his children's thinking.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most, because the date leaves no time for plans or policy.
whatWouldHelp: Early notice, **paid retraining** and a public safety net, plus employers who talk to staff early.
